title: When2Think: Learning Difficulty-Aware Length Control for Efficient Hybrid Reasoning Models
content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence
  [Submitted on 17 Sep 2026]
    Title:When2Think: Learning Difficulty-Aware Length Control for Efficient Hybrid Reasoning Models
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) achieve strong performance on complex tasks but exhibit systematic inefficiency: they often overthink easy problems and underthink hard ones. Existing approaches based on uniform length penalties or rigid routing incur an efficiency tax, trading reduced computation on easy instances for accuracy loss on hard instances. We formulate efficient reasoning as an instance-adaptive computation allocation problem and propose When2Think, a post-training framework for hybrid reasoning that dynamically allocates computation based on problem difficulty. Our method introduces Instance-level Difficulty-Aware Control (IDAC), a reward-shaping mechanism that leverages pre-computed reference statistics (accuracy and token usage) to regulate reasoning depth. Combined with verifier-based rewards and batch-wise standardized advantages, IDAC enables stable critic-free optimization without learned reward models or online reference-model queries. When2Think encourages direct answering on easy instances while preserving extended reasoning on hard instances, thereby learning when to use System 1 (NoThink) versus System 2 (Think). Experiments on mathematical benchmarks demonstrate improved accuracy-efficiency trade-offs: on AIME24, Pass@3 increases by 10.0% while token usage is reduced by 27.9% relative to the base model, and on AIME25, When2Think achieves 40.0% Pass@3, outperforming compression and routing-only baselines.

report.summary: When2Think teaches hybrid reasoning models to spend more thinking tokens on hard problems and answer easy ones directly, improving accuracy while cutting token use.
report.background: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) such as OpenAI's o-series and DeepSeek-R1 generate long chains of thought, but they apply roughly the same reasoning effort regardless of question difficulty: they overthink easy prompts and underthink hard ones. Prior fixes fall into two camps. Compression methods, like length-penalized RL (e.g., L1), shrink outputs uniformly; routing methods dispatch queries to either a 'thinking' or 'no-thinking' model. Both impose an efficiency tax, saving tokens on easy instances while degrading accuracy on hard ones, since neither models per-instance difficulty. Meanwhile hybrid models (Qwen3, DeepSeek-V3.1) expose Think/NoThink modes but rely on static heuristics or user choice. When2Think reframes the problem as instance-adaptive computation allocation and learns difficulty-aware length control during post-training, part of a broader shift toward critic-free RL with verifiable rewards.
key_points: The paper diagnoses a systematic flaw in reasoning models: uniform thinking budgets ignore difficulty, so easy problems waste tokens and hard problems get truncated. It reframes efficient reasoning as allocating compute per instance rather than applying one global length penalty.

Its core mechanism, Instance-level Difficulty-Aware Control (IDAC), is a reward-shaping scheme that uses pre-computed reference statistics, namely accuracy and token usage per problem, to push the model toward short answers on easy items and long reasoning on hard ones.

Training combines verifier-based rewards with batch-wise standardized advantages. This yields stable critic-free optimization without a learned reward model or online reference-model queries, making the method cheaper and simpler to run than conventional RLHF-style pipelines.

Results on math benchmarks are strong: on AIME24, Pass@3 rises 10.0% while token usage falls 27.9% versus the base model; on AIME25 it reaches 40.0% Pass@3, beating compression-only and routing-only baselines.

Conceptually, the model learns when to use System 1 (NoThink) versus System 2 (Think) reasoning, echoing dual-process theory and suggesting difficulty awareness can be learned as a policy rather than hard-coded.
report.impact: For the AI industry, When2Think points toward reasoning models whose cost scales with problem difficulty instead of prompt length or fixed budgets, which directly attacks the biggest economic objection to LRMs: expensive, latency-heavy inference. Labs could adopt difficulty-aware post-training as a standard stage, reducing GPU spend and serving latency without sacrificing hard-task accuracy. For developers, the critic-free, reference-statistics recipe lowers the engineering barrier: no separate reward model or online reference queries are needed, so smaller teams can tune reasoning depth. For regular users, the practical effect is faster answers on everyday queries and preserved quality on genuinely hard ones, plus cheaper API pricing. The main caveat is reliance on pre-computed reference statistics, which may be costly to obtain and could bias toward benchmark-like domains such as math.
report.tools: To follow up, watch hybrid and reasoning stacks such as DeepSeek-R1, Qwen3's thinking/no-thinking modes, and OpenAI's o-series. For implementation, the verl RL framework, Hugging Face TRL, and Open-R1 reproduce verifier-based reasoning RL. Budget-forcing methods like s1, L1 length-controlled policy optimization, and Thinkless offer comparison baselines for adaptive-length control. Evaluation tooling such as LightEval or simple-evals can measure the accuracy-token trade-off on AIME-style benchmarks.
